messages.subject: "Newbie" avian acoustic distance sampling Qs
parts:
Hello all,
I am conducting a multi-species avian acoustic distance sampling analysis,
hoping to model elevation as a co-variate. The study took place in Papua Ne=
w
Guinea and was composed of 6 transects at varying elevations. For most of
the species, the number of samples is on the lower end and there appears to
be significant heaping (as expected with acoustic sampling in tropical
areas). Here are my questions:

1) If there is no or limited convergence of a chosen function (seen when
using CDS and MCDS), what is the traditional practice to deal with this?

2) What does =93some parameters are highly correlated=94 in the results sec=
tion
mean and what are implications?? To deal with heaping in most of the
species, I placed the data into 4 or 5 intervals. I can imagine this could
have an effect on the parameters being correlated.

Thanks you very much for any input.

Best,
Peter Mumford

to
> > be significant heaping (as expected with acoustic sampling in tropical ar=
eas).
> > Here are my questions:
> >=20

> > 1) If there is no or limited convergence of a chosen function (seen when
> > using CDS and MCDS), what is the traditional practice to deal with this?

Distance by default attempts to fit models with increasing number of adjust=
ments. It often reaches a point where it is attempting to overfit the data=
, which is when you tend to see problems of this kind. The solution is to =
use a simpler model, e.g. the one selected by AIC. For small sample sizes,=
this might often be the key function with no adjustment terms.
> >=20
> > 2) What does "some parameters are highly correlated" in the results secti=

on
> > mean and what are implications?? To deal with heaping in most of the
> > species, I placed the data into 4 or 5 intervals. I can imagine this coul=

d have an
> > effect on the parameters being correlated.

It means you're overfitting - see above.

If sample size is small (say up to 40 or 50 detections for a given species)=
, sampling fluctuations in the data can lead to poor models apparently fitt=
ing well. You might want to consider using mcds with species included as a=
factor-type covariate, allowing you to fit a single model to several (pref=
erably similar) species, while still allowing detectability to vary by spec=
ies.

With only 6 lines in your design, you don't have sufficient replication to =
extrapolate your results reliably to the wider region of interest - your in=
ference should really be restricted to just the 6 strips you surveyed.

Steve Buckland

From: Carolina Roa [mailto:maria...@gmail.com]
Sent: 18 October 2011 16:49
To: Stephen Buckland; DISTANCE...@jiscmail.ac.uk
Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] "Newbie" avian acoustic distance sampling Qs

Hello Steve and List,

I saw your response to Peter Mumford's question. I am working with multipl=
e
species using point-transects. I have a large sample size, and similarly, =
for
some analyses I am getting the warning of parameters being
highly correlated. I've been using 2 adjustment terms, in a multimodel set
(combining Hazard Rate, Uniform, and Half Normal), but in CDS. Do you see
problems with this approach I am using?
Carolina, you should not routinely use 2 adjustment terms. Use AIC for exa=
mple to decide whether a model with adjustment terms is needed. Typically,=
when parameter estimates are highly correlated, AIC would not select this =
model, but a simpler one.

I read you suggested him" You might want to consider using mcds with specie=
s
included as a factor-type covariate, allowing you to fit a single model to =
several
(preferably similar) species, while still allowing detectability to vary by=
species
using MCDS with species as a covariate, allowing you to fit a single model =
to
several (preferably similar) species, while still allowing detectability
to vary by species". If I understand, you are proposing using MCDS, filter=
ing single
species, but using species as a non-factor covariate? I know how to select =
single
species through the filter, but is there a way to select multiple similar s=
pecies (pooling)
at the time?
Species would be a factor - you would have to check the box to indicate tha=
t when defining your model. Yes, you can select more than one species - se=
e manual. See the following papers for including more than one species in =
an analysis:
Alldredge, M. W., K. H. Pollock, T. R. Simons,
and S. A. Shriner. 2007. Multiple-species
analysis of point count data: A more parsimonious modelling framework.
Journal of Applied Ecology 44:281-290.


Marques, T.A., Thomas, L., Fancy, S.G. and Buckland, S.T. 2007. Improving =
estimates of bird density using multiple covariate distance sampling. The =
Auk 124, 1229-1243.

Steve Buckland
